This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. text:
This chapter covers methods for producing jackfruit planting material, describing several propagation techniques with their relative advantages and drawbacks.

Seed propagation: growing jackfruit from seed is described as the simplest method but the least reliable for reproducing a desired variety's fruit quality, since jackfruit does not breed true from seed — seedling trees typically show wide variation in fruit flavor, flesh type, size, and productivity compared to the parent tree. Seeds are noted to lose viability quickly and should be sown promptly after extraction (the text gives a viability/timing window on the order of days to a few weeks depending on storage). Seedlings raised from seed are mainly recommended for use as rootstock for later grafting/budding rather than for direct fruiting-tree use when a specific variety is wanted. The chapter gives practical seedbed guidance: germination generally takes a few weeks, and seedlings are typically transplanted or grown on in bags/nursery beds for several months before being ready to plant out or use as grafting rootstock.

Marcotting / air-layering ("ការគាំដោយស្រូប" style methods): the text describes air-layering branches of a desired mother tree to produce a genetically identical clone, noting the typical time to root formation (on the order of weeks to a couple of months depending on branch condition and season) and giving guidance on branch selection (moderate diameter, healthy, from a proven bearing tree) and on the timing and technique of wounding/wrapping the branch with rooting medium to encourage root formation before severing and potting the rooted layer.

Grafting/budding onto seedling rootstock: this is presented as the preferred commercial method for producing true-to-type planting material efficiently, combining a scion (bud or shoot) from the desired mother variety with a hardy seedling rootstock. The chapter describes rootstock preparation (raising seedlings to a suitable stem diameter before grafting), scion selection from healthy, disease-free mother trees, and general timing considerations (grafting is generally more successful when done during periods of active growth and adequate moisture). The chapter notes that grafted trees typically begin bearing fruit sooner after field planting than seedling-grown trees, because the scion material is already from a mature, fruit-bearing tree rather than a juvenile seedling.

The chapter closes with general nursery management guidance: providing shade for young seedlings, regular watering, protection from pests, and gradual hardening-off (increasing sun exposure) before the young trees are transplanted to the field.
